records.title: British Slaves and Barbary Corsairs, 1580-1750
creator: Bernard Capp
records.description: Abstract This is the first comprehensive study of the thousands of Britons captured and enslaved in North Africa in the early modern period, charting their lives from capture to eventual liberation, death in Barbary, or for a lucky few, escape. It outlines the character of Barbary’s government and society, the world of the corsairs, and the wider context of Mediterranean slavery. Using letters from slaves and accounts by former slaves, the book describes the trauma of the slave market, the lives of galley-slaves and labourers, and the fate of female captives. It explores the significance of their faith for some captives, especially puritans, but shows how a significant minority apostatized and accepted Islam, seduced by promises or hoping to ease their conditions. For them, and for other Britons who joined the corsairs voluntarily, identity became fluid and multilayered. The book also explores in depth how ransoms were raised by families and by state-sponsored charitable collections, and how redemptions were organized by merchants, consuls, and other intermediaries. Most families were too poor to raise a ransom, and the state came under intense pressure to intervene. The book shows how from the mid-seventeenth century, the state practised a form of ‘gunboat diplomacy’ that eventually curbed the corsairs. The Barbary corsairs posed a threat to all European powers, and the book places the British story within the wider context of Mediterranean slavery, which saw Moors and Christians as both captors and captives.

records.title: The Jacobite Privateers in the Nine Years War
Corsairs to Panthers: U. S. Marine Aviation in Korea
Raising Ransoms
creator: Bernard Capp
records.description: Abstract Chapter 6 provides the first in-depth exploration of how ransom funds were raised in England, and the roles played by families and friends, merchants, local magistrates, the Church, and the state. It begins by showing how families learned of the fate of their loved ones, and the nature of contacts between Barbary and Britain. Captives of higher status often had the contacts and resources to negotiate ransoms privately. The poor, by contrast, depended on help from others. But who was responsible for providing it, and how? The chapter explores how wives, armed with a ‘brief’, were permitted to roam the country begging alms towards a ransom, or for their own relief. The state refused to pay ransoms to those it saw as pirates. But it became involved at arm’s length, issuing nationwide ‘general briefs’ which provided for charitable collections in every parish church. This system, introduced in 1624, was replaced in the civil war era by a surcharge on customs, the ‘Algiers duty’, but was revived after the Restoration. The chapter ends by assessing the strengths and weaknesses of both arrangements, and compares their record against the performance of the systems developed in continental Europe.

records.title: Conclusion
creator: Bernard Capp
records.description: Abstract The Conclusion draws together the main threads of the book and broadens the discussion to reflect on British attitudes towards slavery and freedom, showing how Barbary coloured political discourse in both the civil war and Restoration periods. It shows how some radicals who condemned the ‘slavery’ of the English people under the so-called Norman Yoke were paradoxically willing to contemplate something very similar to slavery as a suitable punishment for offenders in England. A generation later, Whig pamphleteers warned that the accession of the Catholic James, duke of York, would reduce the English people to the misery of slaves in Algiers. The Conclusion provides an overview of the book’s findings, in particular on the much disputed issue of the conditions experienced by slaves in Barbary, and the factors that shaped them. It summarises how ransoms were raised and how redemptions were organized, comparing Britain and its continental neighbours in their approach to the challenges they shared, the responses they adopted, and the degree of success or failure that resulted.
